The plugin runs in the browser on a RevealJS deck, so nothing on this page can run here.
Each section shows the source you write, then says what the deck does once the plugin has run.
The [preview deck](preview.html) is where you step through the result.

::: {.callout-note}

## How the step orders on this page were read

A slide is described by its steps, counting from the first arrow press.
Each order was read out of the rendered deck in a browser, from the `data-fragment-index` attribute that RevealJS leaves on each fragment once the plugin has run, and not worked out from the source alone.

:::

The [Reference](reference.qmd) holds the options, the attributes, and the rules.
This page shows them at work.

## Annotations as fragments

````markdown
```r
library(dplyr)                          # <1>
starwars |>                             # <2>
  filter(species == "Droid") |>         # <3>
  select(name, height, mass)            # <4>
```

1. Load the package.
2. Start from the dataset.
3. Keep the droids.
4. Keep three columns.
````

The slide gets four steps, one per annotation, in annotation order.
Each press reveals the next marker's tooltip and hides the one before it.
This is the opening slide of [the deck](preview.html), which is the only way to see it: the stepping is the point.

Two annotated blocks on one slide keep their document order.
The first block's annotations take the earlier steps, and the second block's annotations follow them.

## Line highlighting

A block that carries `code-line-numbers` as well as annotations is treated differently.
The plugin reads the lines each highlight step covers, reads the lines each annotation marks, and pairs them up.
A paired annotation shares the highlight's step, so one press moves the highlight and opens the matching note.

There are four cases, and a slide can show more than one of them at once.
[The deck](preview.html) has a slide for each.

### The lines match exactly

````markdown
```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|2|3"}
library(dplyr)                          # <1>
starwars |>                             # <2>
  filter(species == "Droid")            # <3>
```

1. Load the package.
2. Start from the dataset.
3. Keep the droids.
````

Each highlight covers one line, and each annotation marks the same line.
The slide gets three steps, and each press moves the highlight and opens the note for that line together.

### The annotation sits inside the highlight

````markdown
```{.r code-line-numbers="|1-2|3"}
library(dplyr)
starwars |>                             # <1>
  filter(species == "Droid")            # <2>
```

1. Inside the first highlight.
2. The third line.
````

The first highlight covers lines one and two, and the first annotation marks line two only.
The lines are not equal, so the plugin falls back to containment: an annotation whose lines all sit inside a highlight's lines pairs with it.
The slide gets two steps, and the first press highlights both lines and opens the note on line two.

### The initial state matches an annotation

````markdown
```{.r code-line-numbers="1|2|3"}
library(dplyr)                          # <1>
starwars |>                             # <2>
  filter(species == "Droid")            # <3>
```

1. Load the package.
2. Start from the dataset.
3. Keep the droids.
````

There is no leading `|` here, so line one is already highlighted when the slide opens.
The first annotation marks line one, so its tooltip is open before any press, and it takes no step of its own.
The slide gets two steps, for the second and third annotations.

### An annotation matches nothing

````markdown
```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|2"}
library(dplyr)                          # <1>
starwars |>                             # <2>
  filter(species == "Droid")            # <3>
```

1. Load the package.
2. Start from the dataset.
3. Keep the droids, and no highlight covers this line.
````

The third annotation marks a line no highlight step covers.
An unpaired annotation is given a step after the highest step already on the slide, one step each.
The slide gets three steps: the first two pair with the highlights, and the third opens the last note with the highlight left where it was.

## Choosing when each annotation appears

`code-annotation-fragment-indices` takes one index per annotation, in annotation order.

````markdown
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
First, a package.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
Then the data.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=5}
Then the filter.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}

```{.r code-annotation-fragment-indices="2,4,6"}
library(dplyr)                          # <1>
starwars |>                             # <2>
  filter(species == "Droid")            # <3>
```

1. Load the package.
2. Start from the dataset.
3. Keep the droids.

:::
````

The slide gets six steps, and the paragraphs and the annotations alternate.
The first press shows the first paragraph.
The second press shows the code block and the first annotation together, because both were given index two.
The remaining presses alternate, paragraph then annotation, to the third annotation.

The deck has a slide named "Choosing when each annotation appears" that steps through it.

## Choosing when each highlight step appears

`code-line-fragment-indices` does the same for the highlight steps of a block that carries `code-line-numbers`.
The first value in the list belongs to the original code block, which is the state the slide opens in, highlighted or not.
That value is read and then ignored, because a state that needs no press cannot be given a step.
The values after it are taken by the highlight steps in order.

````markdown
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
Set up the two panels.
:::

```{.r code-line-numbers="|2|3" code-line-fragment-indices="0,2,4"}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(cars)
plot(cars, col = "red")
```
````

The slide gets three steps.
The paragraph was given index one, the first highlight index two, and the second highlight index four, so the paragraph arrives first and the two highlights follow it.
The deck has a slide named "Choosing when each highlight appears" that steps through it.

## An index list turns the line matching off

The two attributes are not additive.
A block that carries `code-annotation-fragment-indices` never goes through the line matching described above, even when it also carries `code-line-numbers`.
Its annotations become plain fragments at the indices you gave, and its highlight steps keep whatever indices they had.

````markdown
```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|2" code-annotation-fragment-indices="5,6,7"}
library(dplyr)                          # <1>
starwars |>                             # <2>
  filter(species == "Droid")            # <3>
```

1. Load the package.
2. Start from the dataset.
3. Keep the droids.
````

The slide gets five steps, and they do not interleave.
The three annotations arrive first, then the two highlights.
The next section says why.

## What RevealJS does with the indices

The numbers you write are an order, not a position.
RevealJS collects the fragments on a slide, sorts them, and then renumbers them from zero, so gaps close up.
A list of `"2,4,6"` and a list of `"1,2,3"` give the same result on a slide that holds nothing else.

One rule decides the rest.
A fragment that carries an index is placed before every fragment that carries none, whatever the document order.

That is what moves the highlights to the end in the section above: the annotations were given indices and the highlight steps were not.
It also decides two cases worth knowing.

- A paragraph written as `::: {.fragment}` with no `fragment-index` arrives after every annotation on a slide whose block uses `code-annotation-fragment-indices`.
  Give the paragraph a `fragment-index` as well to place it.
- An annotation whose slot in the list is not a number keeps no index, so it arrives after the annotations that do have one.
  A list of `"1,x,3"` on a three-annotation block therefore steps through annotations one, three, and two, in that order.

## Messages the plugin writes

The plugin reports a bad attribute in the browser console and carries on.
Nothing it reports stops a slide.
Open the developer tools console to read them.

A token that is not a whole number:

````markdown
```{.r code-annotation-fragment-indices="1,x,3"}
library(ggplot2)     # <1>
data <- mtcars       # <2>
plot <- ggplot(data) # <3>
```

1. Load the package.
2. Take the data.
3. Start the plot.
````

```text
[codefrag] Ignoring non-numeric code-annotation-fragment-indices token: position 2 ("x").
```

The plugin reads `code-annotation-fragment-indices` only on a block that has annotations, so a block without them reports nothing.

A list that is shorter or longer than the block:

````markdown
```{.r code-annotation-fragment-indices="1,2"}
library(ggplot2)     # <1>
data <- mtcars       # <2>
plot <- ggplot(data) # <3>
```

1. Load the package.
2. Take the data.
3. Start the plot.
````

```text
[codefrag] Code block has 3 annotations but 2 fragment indices specified.
```

The plugin counts the annotation anchors in the block, so the number it reports is the number of anchors it found.

`code-line-fragment-indices` on a block with no `code-line-numbers`:

````markdown
```{.r code-line-fragment-indices="0,2,4"}
```
````

```text
[codefrag] code-line-fragment-indices specified but no line-highlight clones found. Is code-line-numbers missing?
```

A line range wider than ten thousand lines, or one that ends before it starts:

````markdown
```{.r code-line-numbers="|1-999999999|2"}
library(ggplot2) # <1>
data <- mtcars   # <2>
```

1. Load the package.
2. Take the data.
````

```text
[codefrag] Ignoring invalid or oversized line range: "1-999999999".
```

The last message is written only where the plugin reads the ranges, which is a block that has annotations and goes through the line matching.
A block with no annotation, and a block that carries `code-annotation-fragment-indices`, are both left alone and report nothing.
The highlight itself still works either way, because Quarto's line-highlight plugin reads the ranges for itself.
Where the message is written, that step pairs with no annotation, so an annotation on those lines is treated as unpaired.

## Checking the configuration while you render

Name the extension under `filters:` as well as under `revealjs-plugins:` and the render checks the `extensions.codefrag` block.

```yaml
format:
  revealjs:
    code-annotations: select
revealjs-plugins:
  - codefrag
filters:
  - codefrag
extensions:
  codefrag:
    enabled: "yes"
    patch-tooltip-overflows: true
```

That block has a misspelt key and a string where a boolean belongs.
The render prints both and finishes:

```text
(W) [codefrag] patch-tooltip-overflows: is not a recognised key and was ignored.
(E) [codefrag] enabled: must be of type "boolean", got "string".
```

The deck is written either way.
See the [Reference](reference.qmd#enabling-the-plugin) for why the `filters:` entry is separate.

## Choosing a code-annotations mode

`code-annotations` is Quarto's own option, and it decides how Quarto presents the notes.
The plugin turns the annotations into fragments in three of the four modes, and a tooltip appears in only two of them.

| Mode | What the plugin gives you |
| --- | --- |
| `select` | Steps through the annotations, and opens the tooltip for each. |
| `hover` | The same, because Quarto builds a tooltip for each marker in this mode too. |
| `below` | Steps through the annotations, and shows no tooltip, because Quarto puts the notes in a list under the block instead of building one. |
| `false` | Nothing, because Quarto writes no markers for the plugin to find. |

: What each `code-annotations` mode gives the plugin. {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[20,80]"}

Use `select` unless you want the notes to open on hover.

## The tooltip overflow fix

A tooltip inside a container that clips its overflow is cut off.
The plugin walks up from the annotation marker to the slide, and if anything on the way sets `overflow: hidden` it moves the tooltip to the slide instead.
When nothing clips, Quarto's own placement is left alone, so a `::: {.columns}` layout keeps its natural anchor.

````markdown
::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```r
starwars |>                             # <1>
  head(3)                               # <2>
```

1. Start from the dataset.
2. Take the first three rows.

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

A column clips nothing, so the tooltip stays where Quarto put it.

:::

:::
````

This is on by default and there is nothing to write.
The deck has a slide named "Annotations in a column layout" that shows it.

## Reacting to an annotation

The plugin offers `on-annotation-shown` for this, and that option cannot be reached from a document.
See the [Reference](reference.qmd#options) for why.

Listen for the RevealJS `fragmentshown` event instead.
The plugin gives each annotation fragment the class `code-annotation-fragment`, and the `data-target-cell` and `data-target-annotation` attributes that name the annotation.

Write the listener in a file beside the deck:

```html
<script>
  document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {
    Reveal.on("fragmentshown", function (event) {
      const shown = event.fragments ?? [event.fragment];
      for (const fragment of shown) {
        if (!fragment.classList.contains("code-annotation-fragment")) continue;
        console.log(
          "annotation shown",
          fragment.dataset.targetCell,
          fragment.dataset.targetAnnotation
        );
      }
    });
  });
</script>
```

Then include it:

```yaml
format:
  revealjs:
    code-annotations: select
    include-after-body: _includes/annotation-hook.html
revealjs-plugins:
  - codefrag
```

The leading underscore on the directory keeps Quarto from treating the file as a page of its own.

One press fires one event, which carries every fragment it revealed in `event.fragments`.
An annotation that shares its index with a highlight clone or with a wrapping `.fragment` div is not the first of them, so read the list rather than `event.fragment` alone.

`fragmentshown` fires each time an annotation is revealed by a forward press.
Going backwards fires `fragmenthidden` instead, so listen for that as well when you need both directions.
Neither fires for an annotation that opens with the slide, because the plugin gives that annotation no fragment.

## Printing

`print-pdf` output is a run of pages rather than a deck you press through.
`pdf-separate-fragments` is Quarto's option, and it decides how the pages are cut.
It is `false` by default.

Left at `false`, Quarto's own line-highlight plugin builds no highlight steps at all in a print view.
Every annotation on a block therefore becomes a step of its own, whatever the block's `code-line-numbers` value asks for.
The plugin then keeps the page for the first annotation and clones it for each of the rest, so each note is open on a page of its own.
A slide with three annotations becomes three pages, and a slide with no annotation stays one page.

```yaml
format:
  revealjs:
    pdf-separate-fragments: true
```

Set to `true`, the highlight steps survive and the line matching runs as it does in a live deck.
RevealJS cuts a page per fragment step, starting with a page on which nothing is revealed, and the plugin only opens the right tooltip on each page.
A slide with three annotations and no highlighting becomes four pages, because the opening page is one of them.

The two settings therefore differ in more than the page count.
Only `pdf-separate-fragments: true` keeps an annotation paired with a highlight, and only that setting can drop a note: an annotation shown before the first press takes no step, so it gets no page.

## Options

```yaml
extensions:
  codefrag:
    enabled: true
    patch-tooltip-overflow: true
```

The block is accepted by the schema check, and the plugin never sees it.
The [Reference](reference.qmd#options) says what each option would do and why none of them arrives.
Everything else on this page works as written.
